images.title: The Earth is not back yet
images.purpose: Show that after 365 days the Earth is still a small part of a day short of a full trip round the Sun, and that this 0.2422 of a day grows to 24.22 days over 100 years.
images.composition: One large orbit circle fills the left two thirds of the frame with the Sun at its centre; a single short caption line sits on the right with wide white space around both.
exact_structure: 1 Sun: a plain amber #E69F00 filled circle at the centre of the orbit, no face
1 orbit: a thin grey #6B7280 circle around the Sun
1 start marker: a small grey #6B7280 tick on the orbit at the top of the circle, labelled 'Start'
1 Earth: a small teal #0072B2 filled circle on the orbit, just before the start marker (about one sixtieth of the circle short of it, going clockwise)
1 long teal #0072B2 clockwise arrow running along the orbit from the start marker almost all the way round to the Earth, labelled '365 days'
1 short reddish purple #CC79A7 thick arc on the orbit from the Earth to the start marker, the gap still to go, labelled '0.2422 day still to go'
1 caption line on the right, in dark text: '0.2422 × 100 = 24.22 days'
nothing else: no stars, no seasons, no calendar pages
rejection: the Earth drawn exactly on the start marker, so no gap shows
the gap arc drawn large (more than about a tenth of the circle)
the product written as anything other than 24.22
images.takeaway: Each calendar year leaves 0.2422 of a day unfinished, and over 100 years that adds up to 24.22 days.
images.description: The Sun with the Earth's orbit, a long arrow marked 365 days ending just short of the start, a small highlighted gap marked 0.2422 day, and the line 0.2422 × 100 = 24.22 days.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on why a year is 365.2422 days.
images.teaching_notes: Point first to the tiny gap, then ask how big it becomes after 100 trips before reading the caption.

image_decisions.why: The small leftover 0.2422 of a day is easiest to grasp as a visible gap in the orbit.
